questions.question: Describe the charges of the particles in an atom and explain why an ordinary object is neutral. Explain why only electrons, not protons, move when an object is charged by friction.
questions.expected_answer: Protons in the nucleus are positive, neutrons are neutral, electrons around the nucleus are negative; the charge of an electron equals that of a proton in size but is opposite in sign. A normal atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the charges cancel; objects made of such atoms are neutral. Protons are held tightly in the nucleus deep inside the atom and cannot be rubbed off; outer electrons are held less tightly and can be transferred. So objects become charged only by gaining electrons (negative) or losing electrons (positive).

questions.question: A balloon is rubbed on dry hair. Explain what happens to the charges on the balloon and the hair, and show that charge is conserved. Why does this work poorly on a humid day?
questions.expected_answer: Rubbing brings the surfaces into close contact and electrons transfer from the hair to the balloon. The balloon gains electrons and becomes negatively charged; the hair loses the same number of electrons and becomes equally positively charged. Before rubbing the total charge was zero; after rubbing the negative charge on the balloon and the equal positive charge on the hair still add to zero, so charge has not been created or destroyed, only transferred. On a humid day a film of moisture on the surfaces conducts the charge away as fast as it builds up.

questions.question: Use a triboelectric series to predict the charges when a polythene rod is rubbed with wool and when glass is rubbed with silk. Explain why a metal rod held in the hand does not stay charged, and how a metal object can be charged.
questions.expected_answer: In the series (hair, glass, nylon, wool, silk, paper, cotton, rubber, polyester, polythene, PVC) the material nearer the negative end gains electrons. Polythene and wool: polythene becomes negative, wool positive. Glass and silk: silk becomes negative, glass positive. Metal is a conductor with free electrons; charge on a hand-held metal rod flows through the metal and the body into the ground, so it does not stay charged. A metal object can be charged if it is insulated from the ground (e.g. standing on a plastic cup or glass stand) and touched with a charged insulator; the charge then spreads over its surface.
